items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: one of the guys, Paul Rickey and Will Bradley, used to call you a Communist... He said, what do you mean? I said, I remember five years ago you called me a Communist.

ctx.x: So if we wanted to go out on strike, on the record strike, great. The club date musicians, the theater musicians were only too happy to go make those record dates. And plenty of guys, I'm ashamed to say that I guess they're my friends, though I thought less of them afterwards, plenty of guys talk about joining up and doing record dates during the record strike. The first one, in 1943, I remember, and we had two more since then. And guys would talk about, oh, yeah, I got a record date. "I thought there was a…

So, you know, it was a matter of conscience, if you had any. In the days when things were good, guys would not go to the union meetings. I used to try to agitate to get people to go to union meetings and the result was you got called a Communist. Now, one of the guys, Paul Rickey and Will Bradley, used to call you a Communist. When the crunch hit them, Paul Rickey was one of the most violent, outspoken union guys there was. And you know, very few times in my life I want to say,

"Aha, I told you so." And I'm going to tell you, this was one of the cases, "Aha, I told you so." He said, what do you mean? I said, I remember five years ago you called me a Communist. He said, well, at that time you would be a Communist if you went. So I couldn't win.
